Four-spot megrim (Lepidorhombus boscii) is a commercially important flatfish distributed across the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Field surveys conducted in the Bay of Biscay have documented that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion at approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] post-fertilisation when maintained at a stable water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This relatively extended incubation period, observed during controlled laboratory rearing trials, reflects the slow developmental rates typical of cold-water pleuronectiform fishes. The wet weight of these newly emerged larvae is remarkably low, measuring approximately 0.0005236 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0005236 grams] per individual, a value derived from the egg diameter consistently reported in the closely related congener Lepidorhombus whiffiagonis. This minute body mass imposes a substantial constraint on early survival, as the endotrophic larvae must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The pelagic larval phase that follows is characterised by rapid morphological changes, including eye migration and the initial formation of the characteristic sinistral body plan.

Growth trajectories in juvenile Lepidorhombus boscii exhibit pronounced allometric shifts during the post-settlement benthic stage, with individuals gradually approaching a maximum asymptotic body mass. Data from long-term trawl surveys indicate that the ultimate wet weight achieved by reproductively mature adults is approximately 423 grams [Wwi = approximately 423 grams], a value consistent with the size-at-age relationships constructed from otolith readings across multiple cohorts. This asymptotic mass is attained only after several years of sustained feeding on benthic crustaceans and small demersal fish. The body mass at which females first exhibit signs of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis onset has been estimated at 49.3 grams [Wwp = 49.3 grams], marking the transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to a reproductive life history stage. This threshold mass corresponds closely with the size at which individuals typically attain sexual maturity, allowing for the onset of gamete production. Comparative data from the broader Scophthalmidae family suggest that the length-weight scaling exponent in L. boscii is consistent with a robust, laterally compressed body form that prioritises gape-limited predation over streamlined pursuits.

The size structure of spawning populations has been examined through extensive net surveys, revealing consistent patterns in the lengths at which key life history transitions occur. The total length at which the majority of females reach puberty and exhibit the first signs of ovarian development has been identified as 20 centimetres [Lp = 20 centimetres]. This length, measured from the anterior tip of the snout to the posterior edge of the caudal fin, is routinely used by fisheries biologists as a proxy for stock maturity status. The maximum or ultimate total length recorded in wild-caught specimens from the Celtic Sea is 40 centimetres [Li = 40 centimetres], representing the upper asymptote of the von Bertalanffy growth function fitted to mark-recapture data. Individuals approaching this length are typically among the oldest in the population, having completed the majority of their somatic investment. The length differential between the size at puberty and the ultimate size suggests a protracted period of adult growth during which surplus assimilated energy can be partitioned between continued somatic expansion and annual reproductive effort.

Reproductive output in this species is tightly coupled with female body size and prevailing environmental conditions. Under the thermal regime typical of the continental shelf waters where this species spawns, maintained at 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved by females that have completed their rapid growth phase. These large, gravid individuals release multiple batches of pelagic eggs across the spawning season, with field estimates indicating that females produce approximately 119,000 eggs annually [Ri = approximately 119,000 eggs annually]. Each spawning event involves the release of multiple eggs that are fertilised externally in the water column. The number of batches released per year and the fecundity per batch are influenced by the female's body condition and the local availability of zooplanktonic prey during the pre-spawning period. This annual output is among the highest recorded for eastern Atlantic pleuronectiform species of comparable body size, reflecting the high fecundity required to offset high rates of larval mortality in the planktonic environment. The 7 °C [T = 7 °C] temperature window is critical for successful gamete maturation and embryogenesis.

Longevity records for Lepidorhombus boscii have been established through otolith-based age determination, with the maximum lifespan documented in wild populations reaching 5,840 days [am = 5,840 days] under the thermal conditions typical of the species' range at 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This considerable lifespan, equivalent to approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years], positions the four-spot megrim as a relatively long-lived teleost within its guild, capable of multiple spawning seasons over the course of its adult life at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The age structure of exploited populations in the Gulf of Cádiz shows that the majority of individuals captured are between 3 and 8 years old, with the oldest fish comprising a small proportion of the standing stock. This longevity is accompanied by a slow pace of life, as evidenced by the prolonged incubation period of 7 days [ab = 7 days] at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] and the extended larval phase. The relationship between lifespan and the relatively modest asymptotic body mass of 423 grams [Wwi = 423 grams] is consistent with a life history strategy that prioritises iterative reproduction over early rapid growth, a pattern common among deep-water or cold-water benthic fishes. Natural mortality in the oldest age classes is likely linked to reproductive senescence and a gradual decline in physiological condition.
